clinicalPearls: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus, especially types 16 and 18, underlies the great majority of cases and drives progression from precursor lesions to invasive disease
Squamous cell carcinoma is the commonest histological subtype, followed by adenocarcinoma, which tends to arise higher in the endocervical canal and can be missed on cytology
Abnormal vaginal bleeding, particularly postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding, together with an offensive or blood-stained discharge, are classic early symptoms
Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy of visible lesions or by colposcopically directed biopsy, not by cytology alone
Staging is clinical and increasingly incorporates imaging, with tumour size, parametrial spread, and nodal involvement determining management
Early-stage disease may be treated with surgery (radical hysterectomy or fertility-sparing trachelectomy in selected women) while locally advanced disease is managed with concurrent chemoradiation
Organised cytology and HPV-based screening programmes with prophylactic HPV vaccination markedly reduce incidence and mortality
Advanced disease may present with pelvic or leg pain, lymphoedema, ureteric obstruction, or fistula formation into the bladder or rectum
reference.pathophysiology: Oncogenic HPV integrates into the host genome of cervical epithelial cells, and its E6 and E7 oncoproteins inactivate the tumour suppressor proteins p53 and retinoblastoma protein, deregulating the cell cycle and permitting accumulation of genetic damage. Most infections clear spontaneously, but persistent infection produces cervical intraepithelial neoplasia that may progress over years to invasive carcinoma. Invasion typically begins at the transformation zone and extends locally into the cervical stroma, vagina, and parametrium, then to pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes and distant sites.
additionalDifferentials: Endometrial carcinoma extending to the cervix
additionalInvestigations: Colposcopy with directed biopsy of suspicious areas
Histopathological examination of biopsy or cone specimen for subtype and depth of invasion
Pelvic MRI to assess tumour size, parametrial and vaginal extension
CT or PET-CT to evaluate nodal and distant metastatic disease
Examination under anaesthesia with cystoscopy and proctoscopy when local invasion is suspected
Renal function and imaging of the urinary tract to detect ureteric obstruction
redFlags: Heavy or uncontrolled vaginal haemorrhage from a friable tumour
Features of ureteric obstruction with hydronephrosis and renal impairment
Development of vesicovaginal or rectovaginal fistula
Signs of pelvic sidewall involvement with leg swelling and neuropathic pain
Evidence of distant metastatic spread requiring urgent oncology referral
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends strongly on stage at diagnosis: disease confined to the cervix carries high cure rates, whereas parametrial extension, nodal involvement, and distant spread substantially reduce survival. Tumour size, histological subtype, and depth of invasion further influence outcome, and screening plus vaccination continue to shift diagnosis toward earlier, more curable stages.
pitfalls: Relying on cytology alone and failing to biopsy a visibly abnormal or friable cervix
Missing endocervical adenocarcinoma that lies above the reach of routine sampling
Attributing postcoital or postmenopausal bleeding to benign causes without adequate assessment
Underestimating local extent without appropriate cross-sectional imaging
Overlooking renal impairment from silent ureteric obstruction in advanced disease
management: Treat early-stage disease surgically with radical hysterectomy and pelvic lymphadenectomy, or fertility-sparing trachelectomy in selected women, with conisation or simple hysterectomy for microinvasive disease
Manage locally advanced disease with concurrent chemoradiation using external beam radiotherapy and cisplatin-based chemotherapy, followed by a brachytherapy boost
Treat metastatic or recurrent disease with platinum-based systemic chemotherapy plus bevacizumab, adding immune checkpoint inhibitors such as pembrolizumab for eligible disease
Relieve ureteric obstruction with nephrostomy or stenting and manage bleeding, pain and other symptoms
Plan care through a multidisciplinary gynae-oncology team and provide psychosexual, fertility and menopause support
Conduct post-treatment surveillance for recurrence and support prevention through HPV vaccination and cervical screening
Involve palliative care for advanced disease
